name: Starter deck — a wide one
note: Copy to ~/.claude/smart-thinking/deck.json and make it yours. Each card is one line that reads well in a narrow spinner slot. Breadth is the point: the surface is a few seconds of idle attention, so it suits things that are interesting out of context rather than material that needs a running start.

cards.text: The famous "premature optimization is the root of all evil" line comes with a qualifier people drop: "We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time." The other 3% he meant seriously.
Knuth pays $2.56 for each error found in his books — "one hexadecimal dollar." The uncashed checks are famously treasured more than the money.
Knuth paused The Art of Computer Programming for nearly a decade to build TeX, because he couldn't stand how the second edition was typeset.
Dancing Links: in a doubly linked list, `x.left.right = x.right` removes a node — and `x.left.right = x` puts it back, because the removed node still points home. Backtracking for free.
Literate programming inverts the usual order: you write for a human reader and the compiler extracts the code, rather than writing for the compiler and apologizing in comments.
Knuth popularized analyzing algorithms by counting operations rather than timing runs — a machine-independent measure that survives the hardware it was written on.
TAOCP's example machine MIX was retired for MMIX because MIX's design had aged badly — Knuth revised a fictional computer for realism.
The "10 bacterial cells per human cell" figure was a 1970s back-of-envelope estimate. A 2016 recount put it near 1:1 — roughly 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells.
Mitochondria carry their own DNA and are inherited almost entirely from your mother, which makes mtDNA a clean maternal-line clock for tracing ancestry.
Octopuses have three hearts and copper-based blue blood; the main heart stops when they swim, which is part of why they'd rather crawl.
CRISPR is a bacterial immune system — bacteria file away snippets of virus DNA to recognize repeat attackers. Gene editing is us borrowing the filing system.
One copy of the sickle-cell allele protects against malaria; two copies cause disease. The gene persists precisely where malaria is common — heterozygote advantage.
Humans have ~20,000 protein-coding genes, fewer than a grain of rice. Complexity lives in regulation and splicing, not gene count.

Nearly every banana you've eaten is a Cavendish clone, genetically identical. Its predecessor, the Gros Michel, was wiped out commercially by a fungus — and the same thing is now happening to Cavendish.
Trees trade sugar for phosphorus with fungal networks threading the soil, and can pass carbon to neighbors through them. The "wood wide web" framing is contested; the trading is not.
Tardigrades survive vacuum and extreme radiation by expelling nearly all their water and turning their cytoplasm into a glass-like solid — suspended, not tough.
Bacteria swap genes sideways between living cells, not just down to offspring. That horizontal transfer is why antibiotic resistance spreads across species so fast.
Squid and octopuses extensively edit their own RNA, tuning proteins on the fly — apparently trading away the usual pace of DNA evolution to do it.
A blue whale's heart beats as slowly as 2 bpm during a deep dive and its aorta is wide enough for a human head.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid. Egypt was already ancient to the Egyptians she ruled.
Teaching began at Oxford around 1096 — the university is older than the Aztec Empire, which was founded in 1428.
The fax machine predates the telephone: Alexander Bain patented an image-transmitting device in 1843, Bell's telephone came in 1876.
The Ottoman Empire survived until 1922 — it existed alongside the telephone, the aeroplane, and jazz.
Norse settlers reached Newfoundland around 1000 CE. L'Anse aux Meadows is the physical proof, roughly five centuries before Columbus.
The Library of Alexandria wasn't destroyed in one fire. It declined over centuries through funding cuts, purges of scholars, and neglect — institutions usually die slowly.

Around 1177 BCE most Eastern Mediterranean civilizations collapsed within decades of each other. The leading explanation isn't one invader but a cascade of failures across a tightly coupled trade network.
The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 lasted about 38 minutes, making it the shortest recorded war in history.
Nintendo was founded in 1889 making handmade playing cards, and tried instant rice and love hotels before landing on video games.
The Rosetta Stone worked because it repeated one decree in three scripts. Champollion cracked hieroglyphs by realizing they encoded sounds, not just ideas.
Movable type existed in China and Korea centuries before Gutenberg. His decisive additions were the metal alloy, the oil-based ink, and the screw press.
Greenland was named by Erik the Red partly as a recruiting pitch — arguably the earliest documented case of misleading real-estate marketing.
When a foreign card terminal offers to charge you in your home currency, decline. Dynamic currency conversion typically bakes in a 3–7% markup worse than your card's own rate.
EU261 entitles you to €250–600 cash for long delays and cancellations on flights departing the EU (or arriving on an EU carrier) — separate from a refund, and airlines rarely volunteer it.
Many countries refuse entry unless your passport is valid 6+ months beyond arrival. The airline enforces it at check-in, so a technically-unexpired passport can still strand you.
The Schengen rule is 90 days within any rolling 180 — not per calendar year, and not reset by a quick hop out. It's a sliding window and overstays are logged.
Incognito mode doesn't lower airfare. Prices swing on demand and inventory; the cookie-tracking theory has never held up in controlled tests.
Light timing beats melatonin for jet lag: seek morning light when flying east, evening light when flying west. Light is the signal your circadian clock actually reads.
Global Entry includes TSA PreCheck for a modest premium over PreCheck alone, and many travel credit cards reimburse the fee outright.
Airlines commonly release held seats at check-in — around 24 hours out is often when better seats quietly become free without a fee.
Lithium batteries and power banks must fly in the cabin, never checked. A fire in the hold is far harder to reach than one in the aisle.
A local eSIM bought before departure usually beats roaming by an order of magnitude and activates before you land — no queue at the airport kiosk.
Simpson's paradox: a trend can reverse when groups are combined. A treatment better for men and better for women can look worse overall if the groups differ in size and baseline risk.
Abraham Wald argued for armoring where returning bombers had no bullet holes — the planes hit there never came back. Missing data is data.
In many natural datasets, the leading digit is 1 about 30% of the time and 9 under 5%. Benford's law is used to flag fabricated books, because forgers spread digits evenly.
In a room of 23 people, there's a better-than-even chance two share a birthday. There are 253 pairs, and the intuition fails because we count people instead of pairs.
A test that's 99% accurate for a disease affecting 1 in 10,000 still gives mostly false positives. Rarity dominates accuracy — always ask for the base rate.
Regression to the mean explains why praise seems to backfire and criticism seems to work: extreme performances are followed by ordinary ones regardless of what you say.
A p-value is the probability of data this extreme *if the null were true* — not the probability the null is true, and not a measure of effect size.
In Monty Hall, switching wins 2/3 of the time. The host's choice isn't random — it's information, and that's what breaks the 50/50 intuition.
Gödel showed any consistent system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. Completeness and consistency can't both be had.
e^(iπ) + 1 = 0 links five fundamental constants in one line — it falls out of the fact that multiplying by e^(iθ) is a rotation.
Some infinities are larger than others: the reals cannot be put in one-to-one correspondence with the integers. Cantor's diagonal argument fits in a paragraph.
A day on Venus is longer than its year — it rotates once every 243 Earth days but orbits in 225, and it rotates backwards.
GPS satellites must correct for relativity by about 38 microseconds a day. Skip it and positions drift some 10 km every day — relativity is infrastructure.
A teaspoon of neutron star weighs roughly as much as a mountain — the star is essentially one atomic nucleus the size of a city.
The Sun isn't hot enough to fuse hydrogen classically. It shines because quantum tunneling lets protons pass a barrier they can't clear.
The Moon recedes about 3.8 cm per year, and Earth's day lengthens to match. Tidal friction is slowly trading our rotation for its orbit.
Olbers' paradox: in an infinite, eternal, uniform universe, every sightline ends on a star and the night sky should blaze. Darkness is evidence the universe had a beginning.
Almost every fundamental law is time-symmetric. The reason you can tell a film is running backwards is statistical — entropy, not the equations.
Everest is the highest above sea level, but Chimborazo's summit is farthest from Earth's center — the planet bulges at the equator.
Spacing beats massing: the same total study time spread over days produces markedly better retention than one block. Cramming optimizes for the test, not the year.
Retrieving an answer from memory strengthens it more than re-reading it. Testing isn't just measurement — it's the study method.
You remember an answer you guessed wrong before being corrected better than one you were simply told. The failed attempt does the work.
We judge an experience by its most intense moment and its ending, largely ignoring duration. A longer ordeal with a gentler finish is remembered as better.
The curse of knowledge: once you know something, you can't model not knowing it. It's why experts write bad documentation without noticing.
Unfinished tasks occupy memory more than finished ones. Stopping mid-sentence is a genuine trick for making tomorrow's start easier.
Losses feel roughly twice as strong as equivalent gains, which is why the identical choice flips when framed as avoiding a loss.
Anchoring works even with numbers known to be irrelevant — a random figure shifts subsequent estimates. Whoever names a number first shapes the range.
Dunning-Kruger is weaker and more contested than its pop version: some of the effect is a statistical artifact of noisy self-estimates regressing to the mean.
Working memory holds about four chunks, not seven. Expertise is mostly building bigger chunks, not holding more of them.
Comparative advantage means trade helps even when one party is better at everything — what matters is relative opportunity cost, not absolute skill.
Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. The metric gets optimized; the thing it proxied for doesn't.
Jevons paradox: making a resource more efficient to use can increase total consumption, because efficiency makes it cheaper to use more.
Baumol's cost disease explains why live music and haircuts get more expensive relative to goods — wages rise economy-wide while the task itself can't be sped up.
Money already spent should never affect the next decision. That it reliably does is why "we've come this far" is such an expensive sentence.
Rule of 72: divide 72 by the annual return to get the doubling time. At 6%, money doubles in about 12 years — good enough for mental arithmetic.
A 1% annual fee sounds trivial and eats roughly a quarter of a portfolio over 30 years, because it compounds against you every single year.
Veblen goods sell more as they get more expensive — price is the product. It breaks the demand curve taught in week one.
The Maillard reaction needs roughly 140°C+, and water caps food at 100°C. That's why anything wet won't brown — dry the surface first.
Searing doesn't seal in juices; that was disproved over a century ago. Seared meat loses slightly more moisture — you do it for flavor.
"Chinese restaurant syndrome" traces to a single 1968 letter and never survived double-blind testing. Glutamate is abundant in parmesan and tomatoes.
Salt meat well in advance or immediately before cooking — never in the 3–40 minute window, when it's drawn moisture out but not yet reabsorbed it.
Resting meat lets the temperature even out and the proteins relax their grip on moisture. Cut immediately and it runs onto the board.
Onion tears come from a volatile sulfur compound that dissolves in water on your eye. Chilling the onion and keeping it wet both help; holding your breath doesn't.
Baking soda needs an acid to work; baking powder brings its own. Swapping them without adjusting acid gives you a metallic tang or a flat cake.
Caffeine's half-life is around 5–6 hours, so an afternoon coffee still has a quarter of its dose in you at midnight — often felt as poor sleep rather than wakefulness.
Cardiorespiratory fitness is among the strongest predictors of all-cause mortality — a larger effect than most single risk factors people worry about more.
Alcohol shortens time to sleep and then suppresses REM and fragments the second half of the night. It sedates rather than rests.
The "8 glasses of water a day" rule has no solid evidence base and ignores water in food and other drinks. Thirst is a decent controller.
Nap 20 minutes or 90, not 45. Waking from deep sleep mid-cycle produces the grogginess that makes people believe naps don't work for them.
Static stretching before exercise doesn't prevent injury and can slightly reduce power output. Warm up by moving; save long holds for afterwards.
Basque is a language isolate with no proven relatives — it was spoken in Western Europe before Indo-European arrived and simply never yielded.
The strong claim that language determines thought is rejected; the weak version survives — language nudges what you notice and how fast you sort it.
Sign languages are full natural languages with their own grammar, not encodings of speech. British and American Sign Language are mutually unintelligible.
English, Hindi, Farsi, Greek and Russian all descend from one unwritten language spoken ~6,000 years ago — reconstructed purely from patterned sound changes.
"Set" has one of the longest entries in the OED, running to hundreds of senses. The commonest words carry the most ambiguity.
The Mona Lisa became the world's most famous painting largely after it was stolen in 1911 — the empty wall drew bigger crowds than the picture had.
The golden ratio in the Parthenon and Renaissance painting is mostly retrofitted numerology; the measurements are chosen after the fact to fit.
"Impressionism" began as an insult from a critic mocking Monet's *Impression, Sunrise*. Several movement names started as reviews.
Equal temperament makes every key equally usable by making every interval except the octave slightly out of tune — the piano is a negotiated compromise.
A=440 Hz is a 20th-century standardization, not a natural constant. Baroque ensembles often tune near 415, roughly a semitone lower.
Chesterton's fence: don't remove something until you know why it was put there. The reason it exists is often invisible precisely because it's working.
Replace a ship's planks one by one and it raises whether identity lives in material or continuity — the same question a long-refactored codebase eventually asks.
Occam's razor says don't multiply entities beyond necessity — a tiebreaker between theories that explain equally well, not a claim that simpler is truer.
Rawls' veil of ignorance: design the rules without knowing which position you'll occupy. It converts self-interest into a fairness test.
The Stoic dichotomy of control: sort everything into what you govern and what you don't, then spend effort only on the first pile.
Mercator badly understates equatorial regions: Africa fits the US, China, India and most of Europe inside it, despite looking comparable to Greenland.
Russia spans 11 time zones. When it's Monday morning in Kaliningrad, it's already Monday evening in Kamchatka.
Canada holds more lake area than the rest of the world combined — a legacy of glaciers scouring the shield and leaving the hollows behind.
About a sixth of the Netherlands was reclaimed from water, and much of the country sits below sea level — the landscape is infrastructure.
The inverted pyramid — conclusion first, detail after — comes from telegraph-era journalism, where the wire could cut out mid-story at any moment.
Set line length to roughly 45–75 characters. Longer and the eye loses the return sweep; shorter and the rhythm breaks every few words.
WCAG asks for 4.5:1 contrast on body text. Most "elegant" light grey on white fails it, which is why the design looks fine on your monitor and not in sunlight.
Fitts's law: time to hit a target falls with size and rises with distance. It's why screen corners are the most valuable real estate — infinitely deep targets.
A composite index on (a, b) serves queries filtering on `a` alone, but not on `b` alone — leftmost prefix rule.
NULL = NULL is NULL, not true. Use IS NULL, or IS DISTINCT FROM for null-safe inequality.
`git reflog` records every HEAD move for ~90 days — almost nothing committed is truly lost after a bad reset.
401 means "I don't know who you are"; 403 means "I know, and you still can't". Returning 401 for an authorization failure invites retry loops.
0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 in binary floating point. Represent money in integer minor units or a decimal type.
Any retryable write across a network needs an idempotency key. "The request timed out" never tells you whether the work happened.
Exactly-once delivery is impossible; exactly-once *processing* is achievable via at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handlers.
Exponential backoff without jitter re-synchronizes your clients into a thundering herd. Randomize the delay.
A network call with no timeout is an outage waiting for a slow dependency. Default timeouts in many HTTP clients are infinite.
Store instants in UTC, but store future scheduled events with their intended timezone — legislatures move DST boundaries after you save the row.
String length counts UTF-16 code units, not characters. Emoji and many scripts count as 2+ — truncating by length can split a character in half.
rename(2) is atomic within one filesystem — write to a temp file and rename over the target to avoid ever exposing a partial file.
Comparing secrets with == leaks length and prefix through timing. Use a constant-time comparison for tokens and signatures.
Passwords are hashed with a slow KDF (argon2, bcrypt), never encrypted — encryption implies a key that can reverse it.
Nested quantifiers like (a+)+ backtrack exponentially. A regex over user input is a denial-of-service surface.
An N+1 query is invisible in code review and obvious in a trace. Watch query *counts* per request, not just query duration.
If a page makes 100 backend calls, your p99 latency is what a typical user experiences — averages hide the request that defines the page load.
